title: Delhi HC Appoints Arbitrator for Tata Capital After Other Side Stays Away
seo_title: Delhi HC Appoints Arbitrator After Respondent No-Show
meta_description: Delhi HC appoints a sole arbitrator for Tata Capital Ltd after served respondents did not appear, finding a valid arbitration agreement existed.
case_name: Tata Capital Ltd v. Sanwar Lal & Anr.
citation: ARB.P. 1458/2026, Delhi High Court, order dated 3 November 2026
body: Ignoring a court notice does not make a dispute go away, and a recent Delhi High Court order is a clean illustration of what happens when a party chooses that route anyway. On 3 November 2026, Justice Om Prakash Shukla disposed of a petition filed by Tata Capital Ltd under Section 11(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, against Sanwar Lal and another respondent, by appointing a sole arbitrator to decide the dispute between them.

Tata Capital's petition, ARB.P. 1458/2026, asked the court to step in and appoint an arbitrator because the mechanism the parties had agreed for appointing one had not worked, the usual trigger for a Section 11 petition. The respondents were served with notice of the petition. Neither Sanwar Lal nor the second respondent entered appearance or filed a reply, and the court recorded that service had been duly effected on them.

At this stage of an arbitration petition, the court's job under Section 11 is narrow by design. It does not decide who is right or wrong in the underlying dispute, and it does not weigh evidence or hear arguments on the merits of the claim itself. It checks only whether a valid arbitration agreement exists between the parties, and if one does, and the mechanism for appointing an arbitrator under that agreement has failed, the court appoints an arbitrator and leaves every other question, including whether the claim itself is time-barred or has merit, to the arbitrator to decide. Here, the court recorded that a valid and binding arbitration agreement exists between the parties, which was enough to clear that threshold and move straight to appointment.

With the respondents absent and no challenge raised to the existence of the arbitration agreement, there was, as the order puts it, no impediment to proceeding straight to appointment. The court appointed a sole arbitrator to adjudicate the disputes between the parties, directing that the arbitration be conducted under the rules and aegis of the Delhi International Arbitration Centre, with the arbitrator's fees to be governed by the DIAC's own fee schedule rather than negotiated separately between the parties.

What makes this order worth flagging is not its result, which follows a well-worn pattern in Section 11 petitions, but what it signals to anyone served with one of these petitions and tempted to simply not respond. Staying away does not get a party a better outcome than contesting the petition on genuine grounds would. It forecloses the one stage at which a respondent could meaningfully argue there was no arbitration agreement at all, or that the agreement did not cover this dispute, arguments that become much harder to raise credibly once an arbitrator is already seized of the matter on the basis that a valid agreement exists and has gone unchallenged. A respondent who wants the referral court itself to weigh whether a clause is wide enough to cover a particular claim, or whether it was ever validly incorporated into the contract at all, effectively gives up that chance by staying away.

For any company that relies on a standard arbitration clause to resolve disputes with counterparties who go quiet, orders like this one confirm that a counterparty's silence will not stall recovery through arbitration. Tata Capital Ltd, the Tata group's non-banking financial company, is a frequent litigant before the Delhi High Court on this kind of petition, and this order follows the same pattern as several others filed around the same period. The pattern points to how large NBFCs now routinely use the arbitration route, rather than a fresh civil suit, to move a stalled recovery matter forward once a counterparty stops engaging with it altogether.

The counterparty on the other side of such an agreement, whether an individual, a small business or a corporate guarantor, should take the opposite lesson from it. A Section 11 notice is not paperwork to be set aside, and taking legal advice before the hearing date, rather than after an arbitrator is already in place, is the point at which an objection to the clause itself still carries real weight. Whatever merits a respondent may have on the underlying claim, the time to raise any objection to the existence or scope of the arbitration agreement is when the Section 11 petition is pending, not after an arbitrator has already been appointed and the reference has begun.
why_it_matters: Anyone who signs a commercial contract with an arbitration clause and later receives a Section 11 petition after a dispute arises, including NRI parties, guarantors and foreign counterparties served through substituted means, should treat it as a real legal proceeding, not paperwork to ignore. This order shows that an Indian court will appoint an arbitrator and let the reference proceed once it finds a valid arbitration agreement exists, regardless of whether the other side bothers to show up, closing off the easiest stage at which to contest the agreement's existence or scope.
card_summary: Delhi HC appoints a sole arbitrator for Tata Capital Ltd under Section 11, after the respondents, though served, did not appear to contest that a valid arbitration agreement existed.
card_tip: A Section 11 arbitration petition does not wait for a response; if you are served with one and stay silent, the court can still find a valid arbitration agreement and appoint an arbitrator.

TARGET QUERY: what happens if you do not respond to a Section 11 arbitration petition in India.
